title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6654 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: Gold extends losses as strong US dollar and elevated yields hurt. What could change the trend?
body: Gold extended the selloff in the APAC session, although there was no catalyst for the move. The market just continues to move lower due to strong headwinds coming from higher Treasury yields and stronger US dollar after the hawkish repricing triggered by Fed commentary and the hotter than expected US CPI data. For now, the bearish momentum remains strong, and we haven't got any bullish catalyst to reverse the trend. Nevertheless, the hawkish repricing should now be mostly over, as a rate hike in December is widely expected, while the probability of a 50 bps hike remains very slim given that the majority of Fed members favour smaller steps. Moreover, it looks like growth concerns are finally gaining traction, with the stock market trading around last week's lows and Treasury yields slowly rolling over. These concerns are likely to persist and might even intensify as long as the US-Iran situation remains unresolved, and the Fed maintains the hawkish stance. I think that in the current context, a prolonged US-Iran stalemate or an escalation would keep inflation expectations high alongside a weakening growth outlook, creating stagflationary expectations. And this should ultimately be bullish for gold. At the same time, if there's a breakthrough, we could see a dovish repricing on easing inflation concerns, which should also support gold in the short-term.

title: FX option expiries for 18 November 10am New York cut
body: EUR/USD 1.1025 (EUR 4.33 bn) USD/JPY 160.50 (US$ 946.31 mn) 159.75 (US$ 570.76 mn) 158.50 (US$ 724.36 mn) GBP/USD 1.3140 (GBP 250.00 mn) USD/CHF 0.8325 (US$ 300.29 mn) USD/CAD 1.4300 (US$ 268.53 mn) AUD/USD 0.6760 (AUD 501.29 mn) EUR/GBP 0.8350 (EUR 374.89 mn) What are FX option expiries? The FX option expiration price levels refer to the strike prices where option contracts are set to expire. These levels include both calls and puts. When you see "EUR/USD at 1.1600 for €4 billion" it means there is a total of €4 billion worth of options (calls + puts combined) that have a strike price of 1.1600 and are expiring at that specific time (the "New York Cut" at 10:00 AM ET). Traders watch these levels because they often act as a "magnet" for the price. For example, if there's nothing happening in the market and the price is close to the expiry level, let's say 30-50 pips away, what you will usually see is the price moving into the expiry level. This happens due to the hedging activity of the market makers (banks, dealers and so on). As the price gets closer to the strike price near expiration, these market makers must aggressively buy or sell the currency to hedge their risk. This hedging activity tends to suppress volatility and keep the price "pinned" close to the strike price until the expiration time passes. This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

title: BoC's Gravelle says policy scenarios help build credibility
body: Bank of Canada Deputy Governor Toni Gravelle discussed how the central bank uses scenarios to explain how it might respond as economic conditions change. Bank of Canada scenarios are designed to help keep the BoC accountable and build credibility. When the public trusts the BoC to keep inflation around 2%, their inflation expectations stay anchored. If inflation expectations are anchored, that makes monetary policy more effective. By helping market participants understand how we tend to react when conditions change, we can shape their expectations. Bank of Canada says scenarios help make monetary policy more effective. If businesses expect the BoC will get inflation back down to 2%, they are less likely to build higher inflation into their prices. That decision helps keep inflation in check and reduces barriers to getting it back to target. Analysis Gravelle's point is that credibility can change how businesses set prices today. If they believe the BoC will get inflation back to 2%, they have less reason to raise prices in anticipation of higher costs. That can make an inflation shock less persistent and give monetary policy more traction. The tone is broadly neutral for the next rate decision. For traders, the focus is on how the BoC might respond if the data change. The scenarios give markets a way to update rate expectations as the outlook evolves. This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

title: Fed's Daly says inflation has been too high for too long as consumer spending holds up
body: Comments from the Fed's Daly on inflation, consumer spending and employment crossed the wires. The labor market overall is stable, not much dynamism. Employment is broad-based and seeing manufacturing resurgence. Consumer spending is resilient, even at the bottom of the income level. Inflation has been too high for too long. More from Daly: Inflation is high but uncertain how it will evolve Hawkish Bias The tone leans hawkish. The point that stands out is that spending is holding up even at the lower end of the income scale. With consumers still spending and the labor market stable, Daly has room to keep the focus on inflation. For traders, that argues for patience on rate cuts while price pressures remain elevated. Last week from Daly Last week, San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said the Fed would likely need to raise rates further. Speaking at Stanford on Thursday, Nov. 12, she pointed to inflation spreading into services, where price pressures tend to stick. She also said higher bond yields were already tightening financial conditions, giving the Fed some room to decide when and by how much to move. On Friday at UNLV, Daly singled out services inflation excluding housing and said businesses were running out of room to absorb higher costs in their margins. That raises the risk that more of those costs get passed on to consumers.

For background, the US Energy Information Administration releases its Weekly Petroleum Status Report every Wednesday at 10:30 am ET, or Thursday in holiday-shortened weeks. Covering the week that ended the prior Friday, it's the most closely watched regular data point for the oil market and one of the few energy reports that reliably moves crude prices. The headline number is the weekly change in US commercial crude inventories, excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Markets measure it against analyst estimates, with bigger-than-expected builds generally weighing on prices and surprise draws supporting them. Inventories at Cushing, Oklahoma, the delivery point for the WTI futures contract, get separate scrutiny because tight stocks there can squeeze the front of the futures curve. The report goes well beyond crude. It tracks gasoline and distillate stockpiles, refinery throughput and utilization rates, domestic crude production, and imports and exports. Product supplied, a proxy for demand, shows how much gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other products are moving into the market.

title: US October housing starts 1.309M vs 1.245M expected
body: Prior was 1.221M Starts change +9.9% vs -5.2% prior Building permits 1.295M vs 1.377M expected Prior permits 1.398M Permits change -7.4% m/m vs vs -0.4% prior This is a rare win in US housing data and runs counter to rising mortgage rates and a long string of poor reports, including rock-bottom homebuilder sentiment. I would take it as a one-off until further notice, particularly with the fall in forward-looking permits. For background, the US Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development publish the New Residential Construction report monthly at 8:30 am ET, usually in the third week of the month. It's released the day after the NAHB homebuilder sentiment index and offers the first hard data on new home construction each month. The headline figure is housing starts, the number of new privately owned homes on which construction began, reported as a seasonally adjusted annualized rate. The report also includes building permits, which are issued before construction begins and are generally viewed as a better leading indicator of future activity. It also covers completions, homes authorized but not yet started, and units under construction. Starts and permits are split between single-family homes and buildings with five or more units. The multifamily category is highly volatile because a handful of large apartment projects can swing the monthly figure, so markets tend to focus on single-family starts and permits for the underlying trend.

title: Fed's Waller calls for more aggressive action to break psychology that 3% inflation is the norm

title: Why earnings reports rarely change the bigger picture: the macro environment matters more
body: Every earnings season brings a fresh wave of volatility. Companies report their quarterly results, investors reassess valuations, analysts adjust their forecasts and individual stocks can move dramatically in either direction. Earnings reports can certainly move individual stocks, but they rarely change the broader economic and financial conditions that ultimately determine the direction of the stock market. Earnings tell you what happened in the past, while markets are constantly trying to price what might happen in the future. Stanley Druckenmiller once said that earnings don't move the overall market; the Federal Reserve does. He suggested that investors should focus on central banks and liquidity rather than conventional measures such as earnings. Monetary policy influences the discount rate applied to future cash flows, borrowing costs and overall financial conditions. When interest rates rise and liquidity becomes tighter, equity valuations can come under pressure even if corporate earnings remain strong. The opposite is also true. When monetary policy becomes more accommodative, real yields decline and financial conditions ease, investors may become willing to pay higher multiples for future earnings. In other words, the same earnings outlook can justify very different stock market valuations depending on the prevailing economic context. This is why the economic cycle matters so much.
